articles.title: Islandeses votam 'não' e rejeitam negociações de adesão à União Europeia | G1
articles.standfirst: Os defensores do "não" afirmaram que a adesão à UE ameaçaria a soberania da ilha e suas águas de pesca.
articles.summary: Os defensores do "não" afirmaram que a adesão à UE ameaçaria a soberania da ilha e suas águas de pesca.
articles.body:
Bandeiras da Islândia na capital do país, Reykjavik — Foto: Leonhard Foeger/Reuters

Os islandeses votaram para permanecer fora da União Europeia, informou a emissora RUV neste domingo (30), rejeitando a pressão do governo para reabrir as negociações de adesão e alinhando-se com aqueles que disseram que as águas pesqueiras da Islândia são importantes demais para serem colocadas em risco.

Um voto "não" decepcionará Bruxelas, já que alguns funcionários consideravam a Islândia um caso de baixo risco que poderia ajudar a diminuir o ceticismo em relação ao alargamento da UE e fortalecer estrategicamente o bloco num momento em que a segurança do Ártico está em foco.

O governo apresentou seu plano de adesão como um momento de "agora ou nunca", e a primeira-ministra Kristrun Frostadottir disse aos eleitores em agosto que um "não" colocaria de lado todas as especulações sobre a UE.

Os defensores do "sim" afirmaram que a adesão ao bloco poderia aliviar as altas taxas de juros e oferecer mais segurança em um mundo instável devido à guerra na Ucrânia e à retórica do presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, sobre a anexação de outra ilha do Ártico, a Groenlândia.

Os defensores do "Não" afirmaram que a adesão à UE ameaçaria a soberania da ilha e suas águas de pesca.

Bandeiras da União Europeia — Foto: Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters

A campanha do referendo alimentou o debate sobre o lugar da Islândia no mundo, disse a primeira-ministra Kristrun Frostadottir a repórteres após votar na capital no sábado.

"Este é um grande dia. Estávamos esperando por isso há anos, para podermos ter uma votação", disse Frostadottir, acrescentando que seu governo continuaria seu trabalho independentemente do resultado.

A Islândia solicitou pela primeira vez a adesão à UE em 2009, quando uma crise financeira atingiu a pequena e vulnerável economia do país. Um governo eurocético encerrou as negociações em 2013.

A turbulência geopolítica, incluindo a guerra no Oriente Médio e as tarifas de importação dos EUA, trouxe urgência a uma questão que os islandeses debatem intermitentemente há décadas.

articles.title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier
articles.summary: Parenting experts give their top tips on how to make sure back-to-school runs as smoothly as possible.
articles.body:
It's back-to-school time again - and families brace for the challenge of swapping summer lie-ins for school routines, easing first-day nerves and getting ready for the year ahead.

While children in Scotland returned to school in mid-August, children in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will be returning in the coming week as September begins.

We spoke to experts to find out their six key tips to make going back to school as stress-free as possible.

Cerys Parker, a teacher and blogger, says one of the best ways to keep organised during school time is to keep a consistent morning routine.

Her morning starts 30 minutes before her children wake up, for some alone time and a hot coffee.

She then makes them the same breakfast every morning, which they eat together with no screens, then it's upstairs for showers and getting ready for school.

She grabs their lunch boxes and they leave the house at 07:30 for the bus, or 07:50 if Parker is dropping them at school on the way to her own job.

The night before, she makes sure school bags are packed, shoes are ready, uniform is laid out and lunch is packed for the morning.

"We have things in the same place, so the bags are always in the same location, the keys, and that makes the morning smoother. There's no panic about where everything's going to be."

Keep a calendar and plan for important days in the school year

It is easy to forget non-uniform days, sports days or study sessions. Parker recommends having a family calendar pinned to your wall or your fridge - somewhere you can easily see it every day.

"It's an academic year calendar with a space for each of us, and then an events section, so as soon as a notice comes in, I write it down."

This could include things like meal plans, after-school activities or - depending on your child's age - exams.

It's worth reminding yourself of the school holiday dates, while Parker also notes down key days for her children's school year, such as:

Children in Need, on Friday, 13 November

World Book Day, on Thursday, 4 March 2027

She also keeps a small purse of coins throughout the year in case her children need some change for non-uniform days or bake sales.

Find out how their day was in a different way

After school, many children are tired and are not up for discussion about their day, so Will Shield, professor of child and educational psychology at the University of Exeter, suggests changing your approach to the conversation.

"Ask some open questions, instead of interrogating them," he says. "Ask what made you smile today? Or who did you play with at lunchtime?"

These sorts of questions are a lot easier to answer for a child, he says, instead of asking what they did.

Parker suggests similar questions, like: "What was the silliest thing that happened, or what made you laugh today?"

For younger children, clinical psychologist Dr Martha Deiros Collado told CBeebies Parenting Download that pick-up time should not be a "sign of alarm".

"See it as part of the process of separating and loving you, missing you, which is really important."

Introduce the idea of school before the big day

Many families will have children attending school for the first time, which can be just as big a moment for parents as it is for new pupils.

Shield says parents should "reassure themselves" about the routine they will need to follow on school mornings.

"Visit the school, walk or drive past it, bring bedtimes back a bit earlier so it's not just a big start in the first week," he says.

He also encourages parents to introduce their child into the concept of school, through things like:

Trying on the new school uniform or PE kit

Deiros Collado says school readiness is not about "numbers and letters".

"It's about much more basic things, like feeling comfortable and safe to be in a classroom with other children," she says.

Building independence can also help bridge the gap between home and school life, she says, by encouraging your child to do some things by themselves, such as zipping up their own coat.

"It's just building that sense of, I'm ready to do this without you," she says.

But Deiros Collado also stresses that your child should be able to ask for help when they need it.

"One of the best skills you can give your little ones is being able to say to an adult, 'Help me,' because you want your kid to be able to say that to a teacher."

She also suggests a "goodbye ritual" with your child to practise separation, such as blowing a kiss.

Structure a homework timetable every week

Katharine Radice, teacher and author, recommends putting together a homework timetable.

"Doing this puts boundaries around homework and makes it easier to ring-fence distraction-free time," she says.

This could be different every week depending on different activities, but Radice stresses there should be a plan in advance so it's not left to the last minute.

For supporting children with homework, Radice suggests approaching the task in a "positive and open way" and listening to what they might be finding difficult.

She also recommends looking for opportunities to praise your child's effort in doing work to help them "stay motivated."

"If your child thinks their outcomes won't meet your expectations, they may start to feel that their effort is pointless," she says.

Don't just reassure children - listen to them

Some children who are returning to school may have anxieties about the year ahead, and Shield recommends to sit with your child and listen to their concerns.

"Don't immediately reassure them by saying, 'You'll be fine,'" he says.

"The child's got no evidence they will be fine because they're worried."

He suggests phrases such as "I can see you're worried" to make a child feel listened to. It is also worth trying to dig deeper to find out what is making them worried about school specifically.

He also recommends some gentle encouragement of positive things they like about school to ease some worries, such as lunchtime or playing sports with friends.

If anxiety does become overwhelming for them, if they aren't sleeping or it is stopping them from doing everyday things, then Shield recommends talking to the school or a local GP.

articles.title: I was told I was unworthy to be a mother. Then they stole my baby
articles.summary: Marion McMillan was one of about 250,000 women who were forced to have their babies adopted between 1949 and 1976.
articles.body:
Marion McMillan was 17, pregnant and unmarried, when she made her first trip to England from her home in the south-west of Scotland.

It was 1966 and she was sent by her family to a maternity home run by the Salvation Army more than 150 miles away, in Newcastle-upon-Tyne.

The young mum spent nine months with her baby - a beautiful boy with "gorgeous wee black hair" - before he was taken from her.

She begged staff to let her keep him. "I said 'please help me keep my baby, don't let them take my baby, please' and he was gone," she told a new BBC documentary, Stolen Babies.

Warning: This story contains racist language and descriptions of sexual abuse and violence

It tells the stories of some of the 250,000 women who were forced to hand over their newborns for adoption between 1949 and 1976.

They were powerless against the will of the state, social workers and religious organisations, and the system which supplied infants to adoptive families.

"Let's face it, we were working class unmarried girls having babies that were being adopted by middle class women," another victim, Ann Keen, told the programme.

For years many of the women kept their ordeal - their shame - secret.

In July, outgoing prime minister Sir Keir Starmer issued a formal apology to those mothers, telling them: "The shame is not yours... the shame is ours."

Marion's story: 'They cannae take my baby away from me'

Marion grew up in Stranraer in the 1960s where she fell for an older man who had emigrated from Pakistan.

"I was in love at the time and it was so lovely, I never gave it a second thought," she said.

"We were only together just a few short times, and I'd never told my family but at 17 I became pregnant out of wedlock."

She hoped they would marry but her boyfriend knew their relationship would not be accepted.

"Nobody will want you to go with a black man, Marion," he told her.

In their last conversation, he suggested emigrating to Hawaii where he believed mixed-race marriages were more acceptable.

"I never saw him ever again after that," she said. "Didn't know what was ahead of me. The conveyor belt of 'unwed mother' took control, and that was when I lost control."

She gave birth at Hopedene, a home for unmarried mothers where conditions were austere and treatment could be brutal.

"Everything, from the minute you cross their threshold, is that you're unworthy to be a mother and we're taking your baby from you," Marion said.

"It's going for adoption. So you better get used to that, girl, because you've no money, you've no place to live, you've not got anybody to support you."

While giving birth she was slapped across the face by the matron for trying to get off a bed.

"And I don't know what was worse, the shock of her doing that [or] being in heavy labour," she said. "And the next thing my son is born."

She wasn't allowed to hold him until the following day.

"I was absolutely terrified," Marion said. "Absolutely terrified that they're taking my baby. They cannae take my baby away from me."

But Marion got to spend longer with her baby than some of the other girls in mother and baby homes across the UK.

"I was a Scotch girl with a half-caste, that's what the Salvation Army recognised me to be," Marion said.

"And of course you were told that half-caste is very rarely successful in adoption."

He was nine months old when he was picked out by his adoptive parents. Marion compared the wait to hand him over to death row.

"[The matron] took him, and she was weeping with me, and she must have had another member of staff that took him then, and she was still holding me."

Her desperate pleas to keep the baby were ignored.

Unwelcome back home in Stranraer, she ended up in a women's hostel in Glasgow.

"Suddenly I'm banished from where I was born and brought up and I'm entirely on my own again," she told BBC Scotland News.

Marion was finally reunited with her son in 2004, but her experience as a teenager continues to cast a long shadow.

"It's been painful for him, painful for me, painful for his [adoptive] parents, painful for everybody.

"But it you take away the pain it's been a gift from God because all the years I missed him."

Ann Keen: 'I was told I'd never see him again'

Ann Keen was 17 and working in a toilet roll factory in Ewloe, Flintshire, when she was asked out by a handsome salesman.

"That's when it happened. In today's terms it was without consent. You didn't say that in the 60s," she said.

Like Marion, she was sent away so the problem could be "dealt with". She gave birth at an NHS hospital in Swansea, where she was denied pain relief.

"I was told I wouldn't have anything for pain because I would remember it, and I wouldn't be a bad girl again," she said.

"They saw me as a woman that didn't have any morality and therefore I wasn't worthy of any help. And I don't believe, had I been married that that would have happened."

Ann was told that she could spend 10 days with her baby but on the eighth day she went to the nursery and he wasn't there.

A "cruel" midwife told her: "He's waiting for his new mummy. You'll never see him again."

She took her to a Victorian bathroom, put her in the bath and grabbed her breast.

The midwife told Ann: "I'm getting rid of this milk, you won't be needing it."

"And that's when I knew I'd lost everything," Ann said.

Joan Chambers: 'Teachers are supposed to be trustworthy'

Joan Chambers was a 14-year-old schoolgirl in Sunderland when she realised she was pregnant.

A teacher had starting asking her to go for walks in the countryside.

"I wasn't alarmed by it, because, you know, he was a teacher and teachers are supposed to be trustworthy. I trusted him, I really did."

One day he raped her. "All I remember is the pain," she said. "I didn't understand what was happening."

Five weeks before giving birth, she had to give evidence against the man in court.

Years later she discovered archives that showed that the judge had told the jury not to believe her testimony.

She told the documentary that the judge said: "He's got a good career ahead of him, so don't let her being pregnant sway you."

She went on: "That hurt. It really hurt when I read that years later. For a judge to say that."

Joan spent the last few weeks of her pregancy at a mother and baby home - but she said she had "blanked out" the birth.

"It must have been so painful. I wasn't given painkillers or anything like that, " she added.

"The next thing I remember is like my legs were up in stirrups, a green cover over my legs, waiting for the doctor to come and stitch me. I had been torn to shreds, absolutely torn to shreds."

Her baby was taken when he was three weeks old, a week before Christmas.

"They took him from me and then they told me to go back in the nursery and take the bedding out of his cot and get it ready for the next baby," she said.

Joan was 66 when they were finally reunited.

"It was amazing, but it was so sad," she said. "He'd never looked for me because he had a happy adoption."

'The apologies prove we weren't to blame'

In 2023, Nicola Sturgeon described Marion McMillan as "one of the most ardent campaigners" as she formally apologised for the role of the state in the forced adoptions.

"It was always cruel, unjust and profoundly wrong," Scotland's first minister said.

In an updated apology published on Friday, The Salvation Army said it was "profoundly sorry and deeply ashamed" that vulnerable young women did not get the help they needed in their mother and baby homes.

"We know we must be held accountable for those we let down and reflect on our role in a society that worked against pregnant unmarried women," its territorial leaders, commissioners Paul and Jenine Main, added.

Marion says still more can be done. She wants more support for the victims of forced adoption - mothers, children and adoptive parents.

And she would like to see a centre of excellence for adoption in Scotland, where anyone involved in adoption can receive comprehensive training and support.

Ann Keen was among a small group of mothers invited to Downing Street ahead of Starmer's apology on behalf of the UK government .

"The apology to me means I'm no longer presumed guilty of something I didn't do, because I didn't give him away. He was taken," she said.

"It will prove to the world that it wasn't our fault. We weren't to blame. The state was to blame, the churches were to blame, and we will be free."

If you or someone you know has been affected by sexual abuse or violence, you can find details of organisations that can help at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Risk of lake burst near Nepal disaster site wanes
articles.summary: South Asia News: The threat of a lake formed after a glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border, where a devastating flood struck earlier this week, has eas.
articles.body: The threat of a lake formed after a glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border, where a devastating flood struck earlier this week, has eased, Chinese authorities said on Saturday, as it appears to have shrunk. Satellite images from Thursday to Saturday morning suggest that water in the lake, which straddles the border between China’s Tibet region and Nepal at the confluence of two rivers, has been slowly flowing out and gradually reducing the reservoir, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.By Saturday afternoon, parts of the lake bed had become visible, CCTV reported.The ministry said satellite imagery of the lake on the Purepu Tsangpo river showed it covered 99,000 square metres early on Saturday, roughly the size of 14 soccer pitches, having shrunk by 21,000 square metres since Thursday.Experts and authorities have warned of an extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, particularly from the lake formed by glacier debris, which could threaten rescue operations downstream. articles.body: Franco Fontana, an Italian photographer famous for turning landscapes into abstract images through the masterful use of colour, geometry and shadows, has died at the age of 92, Italian media reported on Saturday.Starting his career in the 1960s, when black and white still dominated fine art photography, Fontana was a pioneer of colour, influenced by abstract expressionism and minimalism. Some of his best-known pictures — showing southern Italian beaches or countryside in stark, bright colours, sometimes featuring a single tree, cloud or human shadow — evoked the work of abstract painter Mark Rothko. “I believe that (photography) should not document reality, but interpret it,” he said in a statement for his 2014 “Full Color” exhibition.Fontana was also celebrated for his urban landscapes, both in Italy and the United States, which typically played with stark lines, shadows, and details of parked cars, and for his nude photography. Born in Modena, northern Italy, on Dec 9, 1933, Fontana never left his hometown, turning down an offer to move to New York while working for Vogue America.This is based on a Reuters report.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Venezuela says it retains ‘sovereignty’ following US oil deal
articles.summary: Under the deal, $19 from every barrel of oil sold to the US will flow to Caracas, interim President Rodriguez says.
articles.body:
Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez says the country is preserving its sovereignty despite the announcement that it will hand over the rights to billions of barrels of its oil to the United States.

The “historic” deal with Washington to hand over 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil will last 25 years and allow Venezuela to develop its oil industry while preserving “ownership of and sovereignty” of its resources, Rodriguez said in a televised address on Saturday.

The project envisages the development of 17 strategic oilfields with an initial production target of 1.5 million barrels per day, she said.

The broader plan also includes the development of eight greenfield oil blocks as part of a wider expansion of the country’s energy sector.

Under the deal, $19 from every barrel of oil produced and sold to the US will flow to Caracas, an arrangement that could be worth $209bn per year to Venezuela, depending on oil prices, Rodriguez said.

Venezuela will keep ownership of its natural resources “while leveraging capital, technology and operational expertise to support the recovery of a strategic industry that has been severely affected by sanctions”, she said.

On Friday, US President Donald Trump announced plans for Washington to take partial control of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves in a deal that would see foreign companies, including US ones, rescue Venezuela’s dilapidated energy infrastructure.

Venezuelan officials are preparing to sign agreements next week that will grant new oil exploration and production rights to several companies, including US firm Chevron, the Reuters news agency reported.

Caracas has been under pressure to act in line with Washington’s demands since January, after US special forces abducted then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and handed leadership over to his vice president, Rodriguez.

articles.title: Iceland on track to reject EU referendum as counting nears end
articles.summary: Broadcaster RUV reports the nation is on track to reject resuming EU membership talks as the final votes are tallied.
articles.body:
Iceland has voted against resuming membership talks with the European Union, public broadcaster RUV has reported, with just one constituency's votes left to count.

It reported that 52.5% of the 188,496 votes so far counted had rejected the government's proposal, while 47.5% had said yes. Some 9,500 votes separated them.

Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government promised to hold a referendum by 2027, but brought it forward because of international tensions, including US President Donald Trump's threats against Greenland.

However, debate in this island nation of almost 400,000 people centred more on its fishing industry rather than security concerns.

Already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone, EU membership would bring Iceland into the customs union and eventually the euro.

Iceland began its application to join the EU in 2009 in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system.

Its application was already well advanced when a eurosceptic government came to power in 2013 and put talks on hold. Fishing rights was the biggest obstacle then - as it remains today.

Fish and marine industries account for almost 40% of Iceland's exports and many No voters feared they would cede some control of their lucrative fishing grounds under the EU's common fisheries policy.

The referendum campaign has fuelled debate about Iceland's place in the world, Frostadottir said after casting her ballot in the capital on Saturday.

"This is a great day, we've been waiting for this for years to be able to have a vote," Frostadottir said, adding that her government would continue its work regardless of the outcome.

The question on the ballot was: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"

A Yes vote would not be a final decision on joining the EU, but a move towards an accession agreement, which would then have to be approved by a second referendum.

Equally, the No vote would not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.

While economic issues dominated the referendum campaigns, security concerns also featured.

Iceland is a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.

The country has backed Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have been alarmed by Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island.

Trump's expressed interest in taking over Greenland has also raised concerns.

articles.title: DNA, unique IDs and geo-tags: How Nepal plans to identify flood victims after burial
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal will collect and preserve DNA samples and other identifying information from victims whose bodies cannot be immediately identified before their .
articles.body: Nepal will collect and preserve DNA samples and other identifying information from victims whose bodies cannot be immediately identified before their remains are buried by the state, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Saturday.The measure comes as authorities continue to search for nearly 3,000 people missing after a devastating flood in the Himalayan region bordering Tibet. The disaster has killed more than 680 people in Nepal and Tibet.Nearly 3,000 people remain missing, including about 2,426 in Nepal and 546 in Tibet's Gyirong County. At least 540 foreign nationals are among those missing.Triggered by a glacier collapse, a torrent of rock, ice, mud and debris swept through mountain river systems on Wednesday, engulfing villages and destroying buildings, bridges and power infrastructure.DNA samples before burialSome of the bodies recovered by rescuers have decomposed beyond recognition, making immediate identification difficult. Authorities have said such remains will be buried after completing the required legal formalities because of health risks and concerns over possible disease outbreaks.In a social media update on rescue and relief operations, Shah said bodies that could not be identified immediately would be handled under government guidelines governing unidentified and unclaimed remains.However, authorities will first preserve DNA samples and other information that could help establish the victims' identities later."DNA samples will be collected, and the bodies will be buried in an open space," the Chitwan district administration said in a notice.Bodies that have been identified by families are being handed over to them.The process is intended to preserve an identification trail even when the condition of recovered remains makes visual identification impossible.Families await newsIn Kathmandu, relatives of missing people gathered outside Maharajgunj Medical Campus, where some recovered bodies were taken. Some searched through photographs displayed on gates and boundary walls in the hope of identifying loved ones.The scale of the disaster has also left families abroad waiting for information. In Malaysia, relatives of 91 citizens listed as "uncontactable" across Nepal and Tibet were awaiting updates.Manivannan Rethinam, a representative for some of the families, urged Malaysia's foreign ministry to establish a communication channel to provide faster information, describing the wait as "profoundly painful".Malaysia's foreign ministry said search, rescue and verification efforts were continuing, while India's Ministry of External Affairs said 275 Indian nationals were missing.Rescue effort resumesSearch and rescue operations resumed on Saturday afternoon after rain and fog had temporarily halted efforts in Nepal."Helicopters are flying and the operation resumed following some improvement in weather," a police officer in the worst-hit Rasuwa district said, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media.Rescue operations had also been suspended on Friday after a lake formed across the Nepal-China border began overflowing into the Lhende Khola and Trishuli rivers.By Saturday, the immediate risk had eased, with Chinese authorities and state broadcaster CCTV reporting that parts of the lake bed had become visible. Satellite imagery indicated that the lake was gradually shrinking as water drained away.Nepal is monitoring two upstream lakes, with officials warning that flood risks will continue until both have fully drained.Nepal seeks specialist helpNepal has appealed for specialist international assistance as it confronts the challenges of rescue, recovery and identification.Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the country needed technical support to rescue people trapped in tunnels, restore transport and communication links damaged by destroyed bridges, identify bodies, conduct DNA testing and preserve remains for longer periods.A team of Indian tunnel experts arrived in Nepal on Saturday, while China has also dispatched tunnel specialists to assist with rescue operations.India has sent three flights carrying 60 tonnes of relief supplies, including food, medicines and blankets. It has also offered disaster-response personnel, prefabricated bridges and technical teams to help restore connectivity.In Tibet, Chinese authorities are continuing efforts to locate more than 500 people still missing. Rescuers reached the badly damaged Gyirong border crossing complex on Friday, using ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads were destroyed.More than 50 rescue workers searched through rubble, boulders and mud on Saturday morning, calling out for survivors, CCTV reported.The disaster has also left Nepal facing a massive reconstruction challenge. Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters that the government's preliminary estimate for rebuilding was between $4 billion and $5 billion, while stressing that the full scale of the damage was still being assessed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Air raids, conscripts and China: How Myanmar’s military is regaining ground
articles.summary: Rebel fighters in Myanmar lose key towns as conscription, relentless air raids and Chinese support bolster the military.
articles.body:
The rebel fighters who abandoned Falam in Myanmar in April said they gave up the border town near India only after running out of bullets.

The fighters had endured a six-month assault by Myanmar’s military, including hundreds of air strikes and a ground assault by roughly 1,000 troops. The fall of the town, which had been under opposition control for a year, marked a strategic victory for the military: Falam is home to the only airport in Chin State and commands a trade route to the Indian border.

Within weeks, three more towns in Chin had fallen, and by late May, the military was claiming control of the entire northern part of the state.

“Falam taught us an important lesson,” said Salai William Chin, a member of the rebel Chin Brotherhood. “Capturing a town and holding it are two very different challenges,” he told Al Jazeera. “Holding it for a long period required manpower, logistics, administration, civilian protection and the ability to withstand repeated attacks, especially from the air.”

The retreat is part of a broader reversal across Myanmar.

The country’s opposition – a loose coalition of militias and ethnic armed organisations fighting the military that seized power in a 2021 coup – has been weakened. Their gains in 2023 and 2024, when coordinated offensives stripped the military of dozens of towns, have given way to a steady withdrawal from the urban centres they had captured.

Analysts say the shift has been driven by several factors: a mass conscription drive that has refilled the military’s ranks with tens of thousands of troops, a devastating air campaign that has killed hundreds of civilians, and backing from China, which has brokered ceasefires between the military and some powerful ethnic armed groups while helping choke off weapons supplies to others.

The war, which began in the wake of a military coup in February 2021, is now in its fifth year. It began following a brutal crackdown on unarmed protesters, with young people taking up arms and forming militias known as the People’s Defence Forces (PDF). They were aided by powerful armed ethnic organisations who control Myanmar’s borderlands, some of which have fought for autonomy since the country’s founding in 1948.

According to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project, deaths in the conflict have now surpassed 100,000, while the United Nations says 3.9 million people have been displaced and an estimated one in three people requires humanitarian assistance.

Earlier this year, Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, who led the 2021 power grab, presided over tightly controlled elections, with major opposition parties barred from participating and voting impossible, or boycotted, across much of the country. He was sworn in as president in April, completing his passage from commander-in-chief to head of a nominally civilian government in Naypyidaw.

Min Aung Hlaing now says his government wants peace talks with armed opponents, including in Chin.

The military has opened new operations this year in Chin, Kachin, Kayin and Rakhine States, and according to ISP-Myanmar, an independent think tank, it has now retaken 22 of the 101 towns it lost after the coup. That amounts to 9 percent of the lost territory, but the areas are strategically located and include key trade corridors linking border areas to central Myanmar, where the military’s main bases are located.

Their capture has disrupted the “economic and logistical capacity of many resistance groups,” Su Mon, an analyst at ACLED, wrote in a recent briefing note. While the military has yet to fully restore its own administration in these areas, she said, “the victories have effectively hindered resistance coordination,” pushing opposition groups “away from large-scale coordinated offensives to defensive guerrilla warfare”.

Still, the military is unlikely to score “existential or politically decisive wins” against the opposition, she added, warning that the country “faces a protracted war of attrition” in the coming months.

The Myanmar military has lauded the battlefield wins.

Speaking in Bangkok this month, Min Aung Hlaing said Myanmar was “on the path of democracy and heading towards a better future”, while state media has run photographs of what it described as triumphant troops returning from operations around the country.

Anthony Davis, a Bangkok-based security analyst, said a mass conscription drive and Chinese support have proven pivotal for the military.

Close to 150,000 troops have been added to its combat ranks since 2024 through conscription, he said, with many of the conscripts barely trained, but numerous enough to grind forward.

Pressure from China has pulled two powerful opposition forces, the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army, out of the fight, freeing the military to redeploy troops elsewhere. Beijing also pressed the United Wa State Army, one of Myanmar’s strongest ethnic armed groups, to stop selling weapons to opposition groups, contributing to ammunition shortages nationwide.

“Unchallenged airpower has from the beginning of the war provided the [military] with a crucial advantage,” Davis added, both in resupplying troops and in carrying out attacks against opposition forces. At the same time, “the rapid proliferation of drone technology in both surveillance and strike roles, along with improved battlefield coordination between different combat arms, have boosted [the military’s] capability”, he said.

The air campaign’s toll on civilians has been severe.

The Myanmar Internet Project counted 520 air strikes from April through June, hitting 87 townships and killing at least 314 civilians, including 41 children. Chin State was hit hardest, with 122 strikes, followed by Sagaing with 101, and Rakhine with 98.

Phil Robertson, the director of Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates organisation, said that “the inability of the resistance to counter the military’s air superiority” had weakened drive among opposition forces.

“Air attacks demoralise PDFs and other resistance troops, and scatter civilians who have supported the rebels,” he told Al Jazeera.

Still, the anti-military forces insist that the war is not lost.

Thinzar Shunlei Yi, an activist living in exile, said opposition networks are still training organisers and building support. “Even in the face of mass murder, in the face of massive violations, we have that courage and integrity that we resist, and we reject,” she said. “Myanmar people keep up that spirit, and we will keep on going.”

In Chin, Salai William Chin remained resolute.

“We do have further plans, but it is still too early to speak publicly about them,” he said. “I would not say that airpower has permanently decided the battlefield. It remains a serious challenge, but warfare continues to evolve, and resistance forces also continue to learn and adapt.”

The opposition’s success should not be measured “only by whether we permanently hold every town,” he added.

“Where the military has a significant advantage, especially through airpower, mobile warfare may sometimes be more effective. The important thing is to preserve our forces, protect civilians and maintain our ability to continue the struggle,” he said.

articles.title: PC Harper's killers to stay in jail as PM announces early release scheme changes
articles.summary: Andy Burnham tells BBC Breakfast anyone convicted of manslaughter will be excluded from the early release scheme in the Sentencing Act.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told the BBC that PC Andrew Harper's killers will remain behind bars as he announced changes to the early release scheme aimed at easing prison overcrowding.

In an exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham said anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, will be excluded from the scheme, which would have made two of the officer's killers eligible for early release.

Burnham said extra prison space would be created by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.

It follows months of campaigning from PC Harper's family and former colleagues to block the release of his killers.

The 28-year-old was responding to a burglary in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged along a road by a vehicle as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft.

When it emerged that two of the killers, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, could be released early, there were passionate calls for the government to intervene and block those convicted of manslaughter from early release .

"I heard obviously what Andrew Harper's family were saying, I mean who couldn't? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison," Burnham told the BBC.

He conceded the announcement will mean "hundreds" more people stay in prison, meaning additional space will need to be found in a system that is more than 97% full in England and Wales.

Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?

Harper's force, Thames Valley Police, said the prime minister's decision would be "welcomed by many across policing and our communities".

Chief Constable Jason Hogg said in a statement he hoped the announcement would bring reassurance to Harper's family, as well as to other victims and bereaved families "who continue to seek confidence that the most serious offences are treated with the gravity they deserve".

"Today is not about politics," he said. "It is about remembering Andrew, recognising the profound impact his death continues to have on those who knew him, the communities he protected and those who serve in policing today."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Thames Valley Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber said he was "pleased" Harper's killers would not now be released but added it was a "bittersweet victory".

The Conservative politician also warned there had not been an "appropriate level of resources" provided to the probation service and the police to keep the public safe from people being released under the scheme.

The prime minister said finding extra space would be achieved in part through ending Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences, or IPPs.

These were available between 2005 and 2012, and were given to offenders who pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public.

Once a minimum term has been served, the prisoner can be released only once the Parole Board is satisfied they no longer need to be confined for public safety, meaning many are being held indefinitely.

Burnham said he had applied "common sense" on the treatment of IPPs, which he had "long-standing concerns" about.

"I was faced with a situation where people on those sentences who have more than served their time, not being released when others who've committed very serious crimes being released early," he told the BBC.

"The judgement I've made is the public, in my view, would prefer a situation where people who have served their time to be considered for release before those who haven't."

According to Ministry of Justice data, 2,271 people are serving IPP sentences as of June. Of those, 856 have never been released because the Parole Board thought it was not safe to do so.

Burnham conceded that of those offenders, there will be "individuals who will pose a risk to communities", and said a cross-party oversight group would be established.

The government will table legislation to terminate the sentences by the "end of this Parliament", he added.

Pressed on how many foreign prisoners could be returned, Burnham said it was "hundreds".

The government has said powers will be implemented early next year to deport some foreign criminals immediately after sentencing.

Those powers would block foreign prisoners from ever returning to the country while "keeping those in prison for the most serious crimes locked up for a substantial period before they are removed".

The government is not thought to have signed any additional prisoner returns agreements with other countries.

It is understood that work has also begun to create more cells in existing prisons by adapting space used for other purposes, but that is also expected to take months.

None of the measures announced by Burnham are likely to create much additional prison capacity by the time the first batch of prisoners are released early in October.

The prime minister is said to have taken a "political decision" to use some of the remaining capacity in the prison system to ensure the changes announced today could be implemented immediately.

In addition to those in jail for manslaughter, the prime minister said prisoners convicted of indecent assault offences and death by dangerous driving will also remain in prison.

Historic child sex offences and causing or allowing the death of a child will also be exempted from the early release scheme, while new "restriction zones" to better protect domestic violence survivors from perpetrators released early will be introduced.

Burnham said the additional changes announced on Sunday would result in "hundreds" more prisoners staying behind bars.

The justice secretary is expected to give a more precise figure for how many people will be affected when he gives a statement in Parliament on Tuesday.

Earlier this month, Burnham announced prisoners guilty of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming will be excluded from early release eligibility.

The Sentencing Act 2026 was designed to address the prisons overcrowding crisis, by releasing large numbers of inmates earlier than had been previously planned. The early release scheme is scheduled to start on 1 October.

But it was met with fierce opposition from some, including family and former colleagues of PC Harper.

Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020 and would previously have become eligible for release under the scheme after serving half of their sentences, down from two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was given an "extended" sentence of 16 years for manslaughter and was therefore not eligible for release.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, had described the prospect of their sentences being reduced as "deplorable".

His mother Debbie Adlam told BBC Breakfast earlier this month she was in "turmoil" following conflicting reports about whether the killers would be released, describing the handling of the situation as a "hash".

Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp previously accused Burnham and Labour of "re-traumatising victims and their families with their constant U-turns".

During his early days as prime minister, Burnham announced the changes brought in by the Sentencing Act would be paused while a review was carried out.

On 3 August, the government announced prisoners guilty of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming would be excluded from the new policy.

Prisoners serving sentences for murder would not be eligible for early release.

While Downing Street initially warned it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter, Burnham later said he was "confident" of being able to block PC Harper's killers from the scheme.

It marked a shift from a week earlier, when he said there was "nothing more" he could do without risking the collapse of the prison system.

The Sentencing Act made a number of key changes designed to mean fewer people were sent to prison, and to free many inmates earlier than planned.

The prison population in England and Wales on 24 August was 86,843, which is 97.6% of the total capacity.

articles.title: 4 days under debris, still alive: How a 97-year-old woman survived Nepal floods
articles.summary: South Asia News: Guna Maya Bohara, a 97-year-old woman who was rescued alive from the rubble of her care home, destroyed in the Nepal flash floods, has become a remark.
articles.body: Guna Maya Bohara, a 97-year-old woman who was rescued alive from the rubble of her care home, destroyed in the Nepal flash floods, has become a remarkable story of survival. Bohara was rescued four days after the disaster swept through the country as the rescue operation continues to look for victims, survivors and the dead.Images of the mud-covered woman being carried to safety in the scoop of a digger have emerged as one of the most striking accounts of survival from the disaster. Bohara was pulled from the debris after a four-hour rescue operation and was taken to hospital, where doctors said she was recovering.Her doctors said she was recovering in hospital. Her great-nephew Dipak told BBC Nepali that Bohara looked like “a warrior” who had returned victorious from battle.Her survival came as Nepal's flood death toll crossed 700 on Sunday, while more than 2,500 people remained missing. Rescue teams were continuing operations across the worst-hit areas, searching rubble, forests and devastated settlements for people who may still be alive.How did the 97-year-old survive?Bohara was trapped beneath the debris of her care home after the floods devastated the area. For four days, she remained buried before rescuers were finally able to locate and extract her.The circumstances of her survival have made her rescue one of the most striking stories to emerge from the disaster. While floodwaters swept away homes and entire settlements, Bohara remained alive beneath the wreckage until rescuers reached her.The dramatic rescue was captured in images showing the elderly woman covered in mud as she was carried away in the scoop of a digger.Her survival has offered a rare moment of hope in a disaster that has left hundreds dead and thousands unaccounted for.Others survived by running, climbing and hidingAcross flood-hit Nepal, other survivors described similarly desperate battles to stay alive as settlements disappeared within minutes.In Timure, a town on the Nepal-Tibet border, customs agent Raju Budhathoki initially thought an earthquake had struck when the hillside suddenly began shaking on Wednesday morning.He ran towards a nearby police post, only to find police personnel fleeing themselves. As he scrambled over a wire fence, he injured his hand.When he looked back, houses in the Timure market were being swept away one after another. Some vanished into the river within seconds.Budhathoki managed to reach a forest about 500 metres uphill from the settlement. From there, he watched the destruction below.“From the forest, when I looked down at Timure, I never imagined I would get a second chance at life like this,” he told The Kathmandu Post from his hospital bed in Trishuli.Another customs agent, Prakash Gautam, also escaped into the forest as the flood engulfed Timure.He recalled hearing a huge rumbling sound before darkness covered the market and a black cloud filled the sky. Gautam ran from his room without knowing where he was going.He injured the little toe of his left foot while fleeing but eventually reached the forest above the settlement.From there, he saw bodies scattered and floating in the floodwaters while Timure was reduced to ruins.Gautam and other survivors spent Wednesday night stranded in the forest because rescuers could not reach them during the day. They survived on packets of noodles dropped by a Nepali Army helicopter.Around 10 am on Thursday, another Army helicopter arrived and flew them to Bidur.“Only after boarding the helicopter did I feel that I had actually survived,” Gautam told The Kathmandu Post.When flood itself became a lifelineFor Tulsi Bahadur Bhandari of Dolakha, survival came through a twist of fate.He was trying to escape when a torrent of black mud and floodwater tore through the settlement. Houses began collapsing around him as he ran.The force of the flood struck Bhandari and threw him towards a hillside. That unexpected push away from the current may have saved his life.“If the current had not thrown me towards the slope, I would not be alive today,” Bhandari told The Kathmandu Post from his hospital bed.Survivors return to find their families missingFor some survivors, escaping the floods brought another devastating reality.Sachin Khati, 33, had been staying with his wife, four-year-old son and maternal uncle Raj Kumar Diyali, who ran a jewellery business in Rasuwa.Before the flood struck on Wednesday, Diyali sent Khati to Chilime for work. Khati rushed back after hearing about the disaster.But by the time he arrived, the village where he had been staying had already been swept away.“When I hurried back after hearing about the flood, the village where I had been staying had already been swept away,” he told the Kantipur newspaper.His wife, son and Diyali remained unaccounted for.Twenty-one-year-old labourer Sujal Thapa was also rescued after being swept away from his home in Uttargaya village in Rasuwa.Thapa was sleeping when the flood arrived and said he was unaware of what was happening until the water swept him several metres away.“I was sleeping and was not aware when the flood came. I was swept several metres away from my house, where security personnel found and rescued me hours later,” Thapa told onlinekhabar.com.Rescuers found Thapa unconscious near the riverbank. He had suffered injuries to his leg, head and fingers, while his house had been washed away.He was recovering at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu but still did not know where his mother was. His father remained in a village in Rasuwa, and Thapa hoped to see him.One life amid a landscape of lossThe stories emerging from Nepal are of people who survived in forests, clung to hillsides, were thrown away from raging currents or waited helplessly for rescuers.Bohara's story is different in one crucial way. At 97, she endured four days beneath the debris before rescuers finally reached her.As Nepal's search teams continued their race to find more survivors, the image of the mud-covered elderly woman being lifted from the rubble stood out as a powerful reminder that, even after days of devastation, life can still be found where rescuers least expect it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Farmer fears for kingfishers and wildlife at crowded River Stour
articles.summary: Daniel Bunting says kingfishers and otters are among wildlife affected on a stretch of River Stour.
articles.body:
A farmer has spoken of his fears that antisocial river users are scaring or drowning local wildlife.

Daniel Bunting, who farms near Nayland in Suffolk, said most people using the River Stour are "respectful", but some disturb wildlife with motorised boats or by turning up in large groups, speeding and playing music.

The 52-year-old said the 25ft wide (7.6m) stretch of water was not designed for crowds or fast-moving craft .

"We're having boats on the river from first thing in the morning to last thing at night and they just don't get any peace," he said. "If you get a wake it would actually drown the kingfisher chicks because they're in little holes in the bank. This year we haven't got any."

The river starts at the Essex/Suffolk border and runs across the East of England for 47 miles (76km).

The Paddlers' Code calls on locals to "minimise noise and keep a distance" when near wildlife, particularly during nesting seasons.

Bunting said kingfishers and voles live in holes about 10cm (3.9 inches) from the water edge, so even small wakes (waves) can do "a lot of damage".

He said all wildlife, including grass snakes and otters, were being affected.

Rachel Jones, manager of Fluidity, a water craft hire company based in Nayland, said it was a "shame" that a few people have "tarnished" things for everyone else.

She said her company does its bit to restrict antisocial behaviour at their hub and users were told not to bother any wildlife they came across.

"There's no engines, no fuel, no picnicking, no barbecues, no music allowed on our craft," she said. "It is tranquil, it is a quiet space for them."

Paddleboarding enthusiast Emma Parr acquired multiple licenses for her hobby, but does not believe that everyone else follows suit.

The 39-year-old picks litter from Chelmsford rivers and believes many who use the rivers do not "understand the rules".

She said: "I actually don't think it's the paddleboarders that are causing the issue. I think it's local people that maybe don't have gardens, you know, they're stuck inside a flat, they really want to get outside and then they're coming to the rivers and they're drinking, playing music."

She added that she has not seen any antisocial behaviour in the community.

articles.title: What does the future hold for Norfolk's first wild beavers?
articles.summary: Pensthorpe hopes to be allowed to home more wild beavers after two adults move in and have babies.
articles.body:
On Monday, Pensthorpe Natural Park announced that a pair of beaver babies, or kits, had been born in the wild in Norfolk for the first time in 500 years.

One of their parents was first spotted on the 700-acre conservation site near Fakenham in November 2025, with another adult beaver soon joining.

A few months later, the kits were born and have since been learning to play and feed in an undisclosed area of the site.

So how did the beavers come to be at Pensthorpe, and what does their future look like following concerns about their impact on land and waterways?

Beavers became extinct in Britain in the 16th Century due to overhunting f their pelts, meat and scent glands.

After Pensthorpe discovered a beaver on its land in November, a camera was set up in its lodge. This soon revealed two beavers living together before they were joined by two kits.

Now a couple of months old, the kits have been weaned as "they are definitely eating willow and various things in the water at the moment", said Ben Marshall, the managing director of Pensthorpe.

"At the moment the parents are teaching them how to slap their tails to ward off predators, so they're actually quite independent little beings already," said Marshall.

"Beaver kits actually live with their parents for around two years, so you wouldn't expect them to go off very far."

About five miles (8km) upstream of the River Wensum from Pensthorpe is Sculthorpe Moor Nature Reserve, which reintroduced beavers in 2022, where they live in enclosures.

Pensthorpe does not believe their beavers were escapees, as Sculthorpe's animals are microchipped and its staff confirmed none were missing.

"I don't think they've come from there," said Marshall, "but to be honest, we really don't know [where].

"It's a really challenging one because it's almost looked too perfect from the outside, one beaver, two beavers, and now we've got babies."

He said the reserve's connected waterways meant the adult beavers could have been there for some time.

One possible theory is they were released by so-called beaver bombers , people who believe the animals should live in the wild and release them illegally into waterways.

Last year, Natural England began investigating where the Pensthorpe beavers came from but have not confirmed their origins.

Pensthorpe said it hoped its young beavers would go on to produce kits.

"The local area needs more beavers," said Marshall, adding the organisation had been fundraising to submit an expression of interest for a catchment-wide wild release programme .

Marshall said this would help mitigate any inbreeding issues, but accepted concerns about reintroduction.

"Beavers are such a sensitive topic, and so we're trying to do everything as best as we can to keep everyone engaged with the process, so that we don't cause any unnecessary risk or controversy," he said.

There are concerns over reintroducing beavers, particularly around their dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.

Conservationists say dams can slow the flow of rivers and streams and create habitats where other creatures can thrive.

But the National Farmers Union has said previously that while beavers could provide certain benefits, they also cause flooded and waterlogged fields, feed on agricultural crops such as maize, as well as damage and fell young trees including cricket bat willow.

"Our beavers have not even built a dam, to be honest because they've got so much rich habitat," said Marshall.

He added some farmers had seen benefits because "where [beavers] actually created dams, they've still got water on their land during this extreme drought that we've had".

He said the future for beavers lay somewhere between the two opposing views.

"I think there's naturally fears about losing crops and arable land to flooding, blocking important waterways and will that affect the fishing industry, and there's so many key players and it's really challenging," he said.

Marshall said local farmers and landowners had been kept informed about plans for the Pensthorpe beavers, adding "we've had nothing but positivity".

He said the animals had opened up fen woodland at Pensthorpe by felling trees, creating benefits for wildlife.

"We've got birds and species that we've never had in those areas and wildflowers going through," he said.

Since February last year, the government has allowed beavers to be reintroduced at specific locations in England under licensed programmes.

Matt Heard, Natural England's national delivery director, said: "We are working with Pensthorpe Nature Reserve, the Beaver Trust and other stakeholders to ensure the welfare of the animals and to develop a plan of action."

Natural England said it was aware of concerns from neighbouring landowners and others responsible for land and water management in the wider catchment area.

It said it wanted wild beaver "reintroductions to be sustainable and work for both nature and people", with a robust approach balancing nature restoration, infrastructure, farming and food production.

articles.title: Battery fire warning in Northamptonshire after rise in incidents
articles.summary: People in West Northamptonshire are urged to bin batteries responsibly after waste collection fires.
articles.body:
Residents have been asked to dispose of batteries responsibly following a "sharp rise" in fires linked to waste collections.

West Northamptonshire Council said the number of such fires had increased from one in 2023-24 to 35 in 2025-26.

The increase mirrors national concern about lithium-ion batteries being placed in household waste and recycling bins, where they can be crushed or damaged during collection and processing, and then catch fire.

The Reform UK-controlled council said the fires correlated with a "huge increase" in vapes, many of which contain lithium-ion batteries, being placed into household waste.

The authority has called on residents to recycle small electrical items, including vapes, by placing them in a bag "on top of the appropriate bin or recycling sack" on collection day.

Residents in Northampton should put the bags out with their blue recycling bin, while those in Daventry should put them out with their black waste bin, the council instructed .

In the south of the county, residents can put the batteries out with either their blue or black bin.

Nigel Stansfield, the council's cabinet member for environment, recycling and waste, said: "The rise we've seen in battery-related fires is a real concern.

"We're asking everyone to help us reverse this trend by recycling batteries, vapes and small electrical items.

"Our kerbside collection service makes it easy to do the right thing, helping to keep people safe while recovering valuable materials that can be reused."

Last year, a huge fire at a recycling warehouse in Rushden was linked to a battery that had been mixed in with other waste.

articles.title: 70 rounds of fire, 3,000-round endurance: How India turned a Russian AK-203 into its own ‘Sher’
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: Every working day, 23-year-old Neha Mishra shoulders an AK-203 'Sher', takes aim and pulls the trigger. But the shots she fires at the Indo.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Every working day, 23-year-old Neha Mishra shoulders an AK-203 'Sher', takes aim and pulls the trigger. But the shots she fires at the Indo-Russian Rifles Pvt Ltd (IRRPL) facility in Korwa are not part of military training. They help determine whether a newly manufactured rifle is ready for a soldier.Mishra is the only woman among IRRPL's nine test firers. Her firing range is just a few kilometres from her home in Munshiganj, Amethi, and her job is to test the rifles manufactured at the facility.She is also among those to fire the first AK-203 made entirely from components and input materials manufactured in India, marking a major milestone in the country's small-arms manufacturing programme.For Mishra, the difference between the earlier rifles containing Russian-origin components and the fully Indian version is difficult to detect.“It is the same. There is no major difference,” she said.Asked whether she would choose the fully Indian rifle if she were a soldier, her response was immediate.“Without doubt. We can take this with our eyes closed.”For India, however, the rifle represents the culmination of a decade-long effort to turn a Russian design into an indigenous weapon, from technology transfer and material development to building a domestic network of suppliers.Why the AK-203 mattersMajor General Sudhir Kumar Sharma, CEO and managing director of IRRPL, said the importance of the programme ultimately comes down to the soldier carrying the weapon.“You may have jets, missiles and every modern weapon system imaginable. But for a soldier standing on the border or conducting a counter-insurgency operation, the most important weapon is still the rifle,” he said.The push for the AK-203 was shaped in part by the Army's experience during the insurgency in Jammu and Kashmir in the 1990s, when militants frequently used Kalashnikov-pattern rifles known for their reliability and simplicity.After evaluating weapons from several countries, the Army selected the AK-203. The next challenge was to manufacture the Russian-designed rifle in India.Korwa in Amethi was selected as the production site, with an existing ordnance factory, land and infrastructure, along with access to engineering and manufacturing ecosystems in nearby Lucknow and Kanpur.From Russian design to Indian rifleThe project involved extensive technology transfer from Russia, with around 90,000 pages of technical documentation covering the rifle's design and manufacturing processes.The programme was slowed by the Covid-19 pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine war, with the final technology package arriving only in 2024.The first rifle assembled at Korwa in August 2023 contained about 5% Indian content. That figure rose to 15% by December 2024.By August 2026, all 50 major components and nearly 180 child parts were being manufactured in India.The transition required Indian manufacturers to reproduce specialised materials and components that had previously relied on Russian specifications. These included specialised steel alloys, springs, engineering plastics, composites, coatings and metals with precise chemical compositions.Building the Indian supply chainAdvanced Weapons and Equipment India Ltd (AWEIL) and Adani Defence Systems and Technologies helped develop the domestic vendor base.IRRPL teams, including Indian Army officers and Russian specialists, visited around 76 sub-vendors across the country to assess manufacturing processes, input materials and technology and help address production challenges. Roughly half of these vendors are in Uttar Pradesh, particularly around Kanpur and Lucknow.Testing capabilities also had to be developed in India. Components were initially sent to Russia and later to laboratories in Delhi-NCR, Lucknow, Kanpur, Bengaluru and Pune.IRRPL subsequently established its own laboratory at Korwa, capable of conducting about 76 types of tests, including X-ray and magnetic particle inspection.Russian specialists, including a chief technologist and a quality-control expert, continue to work at the facility alongside the Indian team.“Components pass through hydraulic and electrical machinery in a production process involving 122 separate actions. At full production, individual workstations are designed to complete their task in about 90 seconds, allowing a finished rifle to emerge roughly every 100 seconds,” Sharma said.The rifle's ultimate testEvery AK-203 undergoes firing tests before acceptance. About 70 rounds are fired from each rifle, including two high-pressure rounds that generate around 50% more pressure than standard ammunition.The Korwa facility has around two dozen firing ranges for the testing process.The first fully Indian AK-203 also underwent a continuous 3,000-round firing test, which it successfully completed, Sharma said.IRRPL is now preparing 10 rifles with 100% indigenous content for Army trials while continuing production under its existing programme.The company has already delivered around 70,000 rifles, progressively increasing their Indian content.A young workforce in AmethiThe manufacturing ecosystem has also created a new pool of young defence workers in Amethi and neighbouring districts.Many employees are in their mid-20s and come from Amethi, Sultanpur, Pratapgarh, Rae Bareli and surrounding areas. They include ITI graduates, diploma holders and engineering students, many of whom had no previous experience in defence manufacturing.Among them is 25-year-old Abhishek Pathak, an ITI diploma holder and former NCC cadet who once hoped to join the armed forces.Another test firer, Sachin Dev, also comes from Amethi and entered the facility through an NCC background.The Indo-Russian character of the venture remains visible at the management level as well. IRRPL's eight-member board is equally divided between Indian and Russian representatives. Four of the eight general managers reporting to the CMD are Russian officers based in India.From 70,000 rifles to expansionIRRPL currently employs around 247 people, with that number expected to rise to about 460 when production reaches full scale.Sharma said the target from April 2027 is to produce one rifle every 100 seconds, provided suppliers can maintain the required flow of components.The company has also received indications of demand for more than 1.5 lakh rifles and is looking beyond domestic production towards exports and potentially other weapons in the Kalashnikov family.For now, however, the focus remains on meeting the Army's requirements and completing the transition from a Russian-origin design to an AK-203 built entirely in India.

articles.title: Charity thanks HMP La Moye inmates for work to save hedgehogs
articles.summary: Prisoners in HMP La Moye make feeding and nesting boxes for Jersey Hedgehog Preservation Group.
articles.body:
An animal charity has thanked prison inmates for helping to save hedgehogs' lives.

Prisoners in HMP La Moye, in St Brelade, have given Jersey Hedgehog Preservation Group 20 feeding and nesting boxes which they have made out of reclaimed pallet timber.

Peter Gould, the prison's vocational manager, said the work could help reduce reoffending because it taught inmates skills to support future employment and helped them feel they were contributing to the community.

Dru Burdon, from the hedgehog group, said: "If it helps with carpentry skills training, so much the better, these boxes are certainly saving hedgehogs' lives."

Gould said the project also taught health and safety best practice and gave prisoners experience of using machinery and equipment.

"For some, the project provides a valuable introduction to skills that could lead to recognised qualifications and careers in the construction industry."

He said the project helped inmates have a "sense of purpose, achievement and connection to the community" which was "incredibly valuable".

Burdon said the scheme had developed from a chance meeting with a prison officer at the vets.

She said: "He found a little hedgehog in need of care and we got talking, so the upshot was that I gave them the templates for both nesting and feeding boxes."

She said of the 20 boxes the prisoners had given the charity earlier in August, all the feeding boxes had sold out and raised £20 each and there were just a few £25 nesting boxes left.

"The response from the public and our members has been terrific," she added.

Gould said the hedgehog boxes formed part of a wider programme of vocational projects at the prison.

These included refurbishing bikes for donations to the Age Concern Jersey charity, restoring memorial benches , growing plants and vegetables for the prison kitchen and for charity, and helping create wildlife habitats.

"We're proud of the positive contribution prisoners can make through this work and pleased to see these projects being recognised," he added.

articles.title: People in Jersey invited to partake in architect exhibition
articles.summary: The Association of Jersey Architect said all entries would be exhibited at Capital House, St Helier.
articles.body:
Artists are being invited to submit work for an open exhibition which aims to showcase Jersey's built and natural environment's "identity and character".

The Association of Jersey Architects said it was organising an exhibition, A Sense of Place, at the Capital House, St Helier, as part of Architecture Week 2026.

It said the exhibition would welcome a wide range of work, including architectural models, drawings, sketches, photography, mixed-media images and collages of the islands architecture.

Submissions must be received by 11 September, with the exhibition set to run from 30 September to 5 October, the association added.

The association said the architecture week was an opportunity to bring architectural ideas into a wider public conversation about the island, "the places we value, the qualities we risk losing and the environments we want to create for the future".

It also said inspiration was not limited to landmark buildings.

"It might be found in the corner of a restaurant, a room, a shaded courtyard, a new piece of street or a subtle addition to the background of everyday life."

It said it could be "a physical quality defined by architecture and landscape, or simply a feeling created by our surroundings".

The association said it encouraged entrants to explore what the idea meant in the context of Jersey today.

It said it hoped the exhibition would "bring together different perspectives on the island and consider how individual spaces, buildings and experiences contribute to something greater".

All eligible entries would be exhibited and considered for prizes and commendations.

articles.title: Epping Forest internet fungi foragers urged to 'click, not pick'
articles.summary: Amid fears social media is hitting Epping Forest's ecosystem, foragers are urged not to pick fungi.
articles.body:
Social media posts showcasing fungi picking is affecting a forest's ecosystem, according to officials.

Picking wild mushrooms from Epping Forest in Essex is banned under by-laws but fungi-related content has surged in popularity online.

Foragers risk getting fined or prosecuted for picking the mushrooms, but they can also be poisonous if eaten.

Caroline Haines, the chair of the City Corporation's Epping Forest and Commons Committee, said posts showing mushrooms being collected "can encourage others to follow suit" and urged people to "click, don't pick".

Picking the fungi can disrupt the forest's ecosystem, which helps recycle nutrients, support wildlife, and preserve some 55,000 ancient trees.

However, fungi-related content continues to grow in popularity on social media, with posts showcasing unusual mushrooms and foraging finds attracting large audiences.

Epping Forest stretches from Manor Park to Epping and covers around 8,000 acres (3,237 hectares).

Haines said it was one of the country's most important habitats for fungi and many species depended on being left undisturbed.

She added: "If somebody clears mushrooms from the bottom of a tree, they stop feeding the tree nutrients.

"We want everyone to enjoy the forest and experience its remarkable wildlife. Our message is simple - click, don't pick."

The City Corporation, which manages Epping Forest as a registered charity, said its open spaces had been home to several significant fungi discoveries in recent years.

In 2024, a new species of mushroom, Hydropus inopinatus, was discovered in Burnham Beeches, Buckinghamshire.

In 2025, the UK's first confirmed record of a rare fungus species, Russula blumiana, was made in Epping Forest.

articles.title: Nuneaton' s merry midwives' final curtain after 40 years of shows
articles.summary: A group of nurses have raised around £150,000 for local organisations through their performances.
articles.body:
A group of nurses that has raised around £150,000 over 40 years of staging charity shows is preparing to take its final bow.

The Merry Midwives was set up by Julie Brady and a colleague in 1986. They got the performing bug after they were asked to put together a skit for the former Nuneaton Maternity Hospital show.

The pair pulled together a group to raise funds for hospital equipment, and loved it so much they decided to continue, picking up firm friends along the way.

Brady, now 69, who lives in Nuneaton and directs the performances, said The Merry Midwives - The Final Curtain at Abbey Theatre in October would feel "bittersweet", adding: "We want to go out on a high."

Her first performance with fellow midwife, Maggie Davies, who has since sadly died, was in March 1981, when the pair were asked by their boss to "show what midwives could do".

"We just loved it," the retired midwife remembered.

A few years later they began taking to the stage regularly, at first raising funds for TVs, stethoscopes and foetal Dopplers for the maternity unit.

As their fame spread, the group was asked to perform at the Royal College of Midwives AGM, and a conference in Harrogate, and they also appeared on BBC quiz show, Eggheads.

Over the years they have shared their proceeds with a range of local organisations, including the air ambulance, a singing for dementia group and Mary Ann Evans Hospice in Nuneaton.

The 15-strong group is now largely retired, but ranges in age from 37 to 84, with three working nurses including Brady's daughter, a singer who "keeps us in tune and teaches us some harmonies."

Described as "half a review, half a pantomime", their performances comprise of rewritten songs, sketches and dances.

"We always ask our audiences to bear in mind that we'd never give up our day jobs," Brady laughed.

"It's very fast-moving. We have a horde of women behind the scenes who literally rip one costume off and throw another one on because we've only got three minutes before we're back on."

Abbey Theatre volunteers help with lighting, sound and stage management, and the group divvies up other jobs.

Many members of their audience have been coming back to watch every year since 1986.

Only a handful of the original performers remain, with some "great friends" lost along the way.

"We're just a great group of friends," Brady said. "We've had lots of ups and downs... Lots of us have had near misses and operations.

"I find it amazing that there's 15 of us that have got such a daft sense of humour and have stuck together over the last 40 years.

"Really it's the friendship that's the best thing."

She said she would miss the act "hugely", even though "40 years is a long time to be compiling shows, making costumes and making props".

But the group plans to keep meeting up socially, including at a singing group they have formed on the side.

"As long as we keep seeing each other I think we'll be fine," Brady said.

The Merry Midwives - The Final Curtain shows take place from 1-3 October, with proceeds going to charities Guy's Gift, The Friendship Project and Saints.
