articles.title: Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?
articles.summary: The prime minister says he will keep hundreds more criminals behind bars but doing so requires complex changes.
articles.body:
The prime minister's announcement that he will keep hundreds of criminals behind bars who would otherwise have been released early is one he has wanted to make for weeks.

Andy Burnham had already expanded the list of people ineligible for early release and had consistently said he wanted to go further.

What is not clear is exactly what has changed to allow him to do so.

Earlier this month, the Ministry of Justice warned that exempting any more prisoners risked "prisons reaching capacity and collapsing".

The prime minister himself previously said he had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".

In his exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham picked out the release of people on controversial indefinite sentences and the deportation of foreign criminals as measures that had made his latest intervention possible.

It is understood extra capacity will also be created by immediately beginning work to create new cells in existing prisons.

But none of these are short-term solutions.

Ending indefinite sentences will require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up.

Previous governments have struggled to quickly deport foreign offenders and there are not thought to be any new returns agreements with other countries. The case of grooming gang ringleader Shabir Ahmed, who Pakistan has resisted attempts to deport, is one example.

Retrofitting prisons to create more cells is also expected to take months.

People in government concede that in the short-term, Burnham will only be able to follow through on today's announcement by making prisons even more full.

With the adult male prison estate already running at 98% capacity, it is a move that could worry some in the sector.

But in the end, the prime minister believed he simply had to act.

The extra exemptions Burnham has announced are being described within government as a "political decision".

That is not surprising given the intense pressure that had built up, especially around the potential for PC Andrew Harper's killers to be released early.

Burnham's inner circle are mindful that political misjudgements at the start of Sir Keir Starmer's premiership caused long-lasting damage.

They believe Sir Keir never recovered from early rows over freebies and winter fuel payments, and point to a lack of major mishaps in Burnham's first six weeks in office as evidence of a more slick political operation.

There was some surprise in Downing Street about how much media attention the issue of early release received over the summer.

That is one reason why the prime minister's aides are relishing the new parliamentary term, when news stories come along at a faster rate and so are less likely to linger in the headlines.

After the initial flip-flopping on whether the government would be able to exempt more prisoners, the mother of PC Harper told BBC Breakfast that the handling of the situation had been a "hash".

Government officials working on the plans have spoken to the families of victims, who made it clear they did not want the new measures to be dripped out in leaks to the media.

Instead it was decided one big announcement would be the neatest option.

It had seemed likely that would come in the form of a parliamentary statement on Tuesday from the justice secretary.

Instead, the prime minister decided to make the announcement himself in an interview with BBC Breakfast.

It is understood Burnham was mindful of mounting speculation and wanted to give victims and the public as much certainty at the earliest possible opportunity.

In doing so, he may have risked the ire of the Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle, who is generally disdainful of governments that make major announcements outside of Parliament.

He may also have offered up ammunition to the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who has already accused Burnham of being a "people pleaser" who finds it difficult to say no to people.

That characterisation is likely to be tested again when more stories inevitably appear about the victims of prisoners who will still be released early.

While this is not the first time Burnham has said he has pushed the system to the limit, Whitehall sources are now adamant there will be no more additional exemptions.

articles.title: Not just a phase: the enduring appeal of emo
articles.summary: Sophie Baxter has set up a social group for "emos, goths and moshers" who never left the noughties.
articles.body:
When My Chemical Romance headlined Wembley for three sold-out shows in July, for many it was a trip down memory lane to a time when they classed themselves as "emo" - wearing black, having piercings and listening to alternative music.

But for others, this was never just a phase of their youth. This was a way of life.

Sophie Baxter, 31, from Hull, describes herself as alternative and runs a social group for "emos, goths and moshers" to meet like-minded people who "understand where you're coming from".

"I think people who are not alternative often see it as a form of rebellion or a movement but it isn't, in my opinion anyway, it's just a lifestyle and a way of expressing who you are," she says.

The group, called Never a Phase, meets regularly in Hull and now has more than 2,000 followers on Instagram.

Sophie says she set it up after finding it "really hard to meet people on the same wavelength" in corporate spaces, and how she felt it was important to meet friends "you can be your 100% authentic self with".

She believes people are "very expressive with their style and music choices" in their teenage years, but society and the demands of fitting in at work means those people eventually feel they have to "squash themselves".

But deep down, the desire to be alternative never leaves them.

She adds: "You get to a certain level, maybe as you get to late twenties, early thirties, where you think, actually, I can be an emo, I can be alternative, I can be a little bit weird. I'm still a good person."

Defined by its music, fashion and stereotype of moody, depressive teens, alternative and emo culture peaked in the 2000s with bands such as My Chemical Romance, Fall Out Boy and Panic at the Disco taking it mainstream.

However, this stereotype is being challenged by those who welcome an alternative crowd to events.

Daniel Mawer, who runs the Polar Bear Music Club in Hull, says the Panic at the Emo! night the club hosts is "one of my favourite shows to work at".

He says: "I'd say people who attend this night are the most likely to make new friends, be the most welcoming to outsiders and would probably have the most fun out of all the events we host."

While there is a lot of nostalgia at the events, he says they are also popular with a younger crowd.

"We're noticing that there's a wave of teenagers who are embracing the fashion and aesthetics that were synonymous with the early noughties," Daniel adds.

"It's genuinely refreshing to see young people belonging to a tribe where they feel a sense of belonging. I had that as a kid and it was really important to me.

"It unfortunately seemed to have missed a whole generation due to Covid, but is obviously returning within this genre."

US group Paramore was one of the biggest emo bands of the noughties and performed to sell-out crowds on Taylor Swift's Eras Tour in 2024, including at Wembley, highlighting the genre's longevity and how it is reaching a younger crowd today.

Miguel Raimundo runs Emofest events across Europe, with gigs featuring a live band playing classic songs from the time.

He says the crowd at these shows, with one taking place at the University of Hull's Union in September, are the "friendliest", with an age range from 14 to "corporate elder emos" in their forties and fifties.

He says: "The emo crowd gets a bad rep, but Emofest has some of the best shows we run across the UK."

The life of Sophie Lancaster, who was kicked to death by teenage boys in 2007 because she was a goth, continues to be celebrated through a foundation set up in her honour .

Sophie Baxter says she gave thought about what had happened to the 20-year-old when setting up Never a Phase, but the overwhelming response so far had been positive.

She says it suggests public perception could be changing from 20 years ago.

"The bigger we get, I do have that [Sophie Lancaster's death] in the back of my mind. And it's sad, but sort of necessary when you take things online and in a public arena," she says.

"There's been a couple of maybe not so nice comments on Instagram Reels, but they're very much the minority and it is something that feels like it is very needed.

"We've had lots of positive messages and people saying, 'oh my God, where have you been?' And people finally feeling like they belong somewhere.

"It doesn't matter what you look like, it doesn't matter what sexuality you are or what music you listen to, it's a mindset. So if you're comfortable being around alternative people, around emos and weirdos and moshers and freaks, then you probably belong with us."

articles.title: 'Drug-free India' to 'vocal for local': Key quotes from PM Modi’s 137th Mann Ki Baat
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: In the 137th episode of Mann Ki Baat, Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted grassroots initiatives and individuals creating change throu.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In the 137th episode of Mann Ki Baat, Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted grassroots initiatives and individuals creating change through technology, social action, entrepreneurship and community participation. He began by discussing a digital initiative by Mumbai-based Krishna Sheshadri that uses technology to make Indian history more engaging.PM Modi then called for greater public participation in the campaign for a drug-free India, particularly among young people.He also spoke about the patriotic spirit surrounding August, including Har Ghar Tiranga, National Handloom Day, the Quit India Movement anniversary, Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, Independence Day and National Space Day.He highlighted women street vendors benefiting from PM SVANidhi, citing examples from Ghaziabad and Bengaluru.Cleanliness was another major theme, with PM Modi highlighting young volunteers in Uttar Pradesh and sanitation efforts during the Amarnath Yatra. He then showcased individuals turning personal interests and environmental conservation into livelihoods, including a flower farmer in Nagaland and women involved in ecotourism and forest conservation in Odisha.The Prime Minister also highlighted Mission ShaktiSAT, which is bringing thousands of girls from across the world into satellite technology and innovation. He discussed the growing cultivation of avocado by Indian farmers, paid tribute to Bengali cinema icon Uttam Kumar ahead of his birth centenary, and ended by speaking about Janmashtami, Vishwakarma Puja, Diwali and the importance of buying Indian-made products under the Vocal for Local campaign.Top quotes from the episodeThe campaign ‘Drug-Free Youth for Developed India’ is rapidly gaining momentum across the country. Its objective is absolutely clear: a drug-free youth, a drug-free India. Drug addiction does not engulf only one person. Its consequences are also suffered by the entire family and society. I would appreciate those who raise awareness among others against drugs and come forward to help people struggling with addiction.In the month of August, we see many colours of patriotism everywhere. From National Handloom Day and the anniversary of the Quit India Movement to Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, these occasions make the month special. The Har Ghar Tiranga campaign strengthens this feeling further. This year has become even more special because 150 years of Vande Mataram are being completed.”PM SVANidhi scheme is giving new strength to millions of such mothers and sisters. This aspect of women’s empowerment does not receive as much discussion as it should. Around 46 per cent of the beneficiaries of PM SVANidhi are women. That means nearly 35 lakh women across the country are connected with this scheme and are taking their businesses forward.This year, we saw a similarly inspiring picture of cleanliness and public participation during the Shri Amarnath Yatra. Thousands of sanitation workers remained engaged in service day and night on difficult routes. More than 400 metric tonnes of waste was collected and processed during the pilgrimage this year. One aspect of this effort particularly pleased me.Vaishalu Puroji from Phek district of Nagaland began growing flowers on a small scale. Gradually, she began to see an opportunity in it. During this journey, she received training in scientific flower cultivation from the local Krishi Vigyan Kendra. She then planted thousands of gladiolus plants on just one-quarter of an acre of land. More than 5,000 flowers bloomed in her very first attempt.Today, the dreams of our daughters are travelling from the Earth all the way into space. And you will be proud to know that India is bringing together thousands of girls from across the world who dream of achieving such things. The name of this effort is Mission ShaktiSAT. Through it, 12,000 female students from 108 countries are getting an opportunity to learn satellite technology and move forward in the field of innovation.”During this festive season, I once again repeat my appeal for Vocal for Local. And Vocal for Local does not simply mean buying earthen lamps. Its vision is much broader. Whatever we buy for our homes, let us check once whether it has been made in India. I appeal to you to adopt Vocal for Local yourself and also inspire others to do the same.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Egypt unearths Mamluk-era pilgrim’s inn belonging to lost city along historic Sinai trade route
articles.summary: The discovery at Asila opens a window into the trade network connected Egypt with the Arabian Peninsula, said Egyptian Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sh...
articles.body:
The discovery at Asila opens a window into the trade network connected Egypt with the Arabian Peninsula, said Egyptian Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy.

The remains of a building believed to be an inn for medieval travelers were unearthed during excavations carried out in the previously lost city of Asila, Egypt's Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced earlier this month.

The discovery comes as part of the ministry's efforts to excavate and shed light on the history of the Sinai desert, its cities, and ancient trade routes.

Asila is located in the northern Sinai along the Egyptian Hajj Route, or the Sultan's Road, an extensive trade and pilgrimage route that connected Egypt with the Levant and Arabian Peninsula between the early Islamic and the Ottoman periods.

The Crusader threat to the region halted use of the route during the 11th century CE, causing the pilgrimage route to shift to the southern path leading through Aydhab, an ancient Egyptian Red Sea port , and the Saudi Arabian coastal city of Jeddah.

Mudbrick and red brick walls with limestone-reinforced foundations were unearthed at the Asila site, a method not uncommon in Islamic-era construction, according to Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of the Supreme Council of Antiquities.

Leithy added that the walls, which stretch toward the north, east, and south, bear evidence of having once contained several internal rooms, which may have been used as store fronts attached to the inn.

The site's overall layout closely resembles that of Khan al-Khuwainat, another ancient commercial site found in the northern Sinai, Leithy said.

He noted that while Asila is smaller than Khan al-Khuwainat, the similarity between the two lends support to the theory that both served as rest stops for merchants and travelers along the trade route.

Green-glazed vessels, pottery point to reign of Mamluk sultan

Vessels painted with an olive-green glaze, as well as glazed and decorated pottery fragments found at the site point to the site belonging to the reign of Mamluk Sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad of the Bahri dynasty.

Some artifacts found also bear Arabic letters that may form part of the word "al-Nasir," though further analysis of the fragments is needed to precisely date the site and determine the function of its structures.

Red and white decorated pottery and fragments of lamps have also been found at the site.

Infastructure supporting trade, pilgrimage during Islamic period

"The discovery contributed to understanding the nature of the infrastructure that supported trade, pilgrimage, and military movements during the Islamic periods," explained archaeological mission heads Mohamed Khalil and Saddam Hussein.

It also helps in studying the network of rest stations strategically built along Sinai's routes to serve travelers and caravans, the two said.

He described the discovery as an "important addition to a series of archaeological discoveries that contribute to rereading Sinai's history and shedding light on the civilizations and communities that flourished on its land."

articles.title: One person killed, five wounded in shooting at rave in Switzerland
articles.summary: Police said a manhunt is under way following the incident at the annual techno party.
articles.body:
At least one person has been killed and five others injured in a shooting at an overnight rave party in northern Switzerland, local police said.

“The search for the perpetrators, whose identities are currently unknown, is under way,” police said on social media on Sunday, adding that the motives and exact circumstances regarding the incident in Aarau, north of Zurich, were not yet known.

Swiss newspaper Blick reported that the shots were fired before 3am (01:00 GMT) on the sidelines of the Aarauer Rave.

Some 3,500 people attended the annual techno party between 3pm on Saturday and 2am on Sunday.

Police said a search operation was under way, appealing to the public for any film or pictures of the incident.

Blick published video footage, taken from an elevated position, which it said had come from a reader showing a night-time street scene with the sound of several shots being fired.

Large areas of Aarau have been cordoned off, police said, adding that they have increased their presence beyond the town as a precautionary measure.

Police spokeswoman Vanessa Rumpold told Blick that the shooting happened at the racecourse where the event was held.

“Several shots were fired within a large group of people,” she said.

One witness reported “bursts of gunfire”, according to the daily.

Switzerland has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe, although violent shootings are rare. It approved tighter gun control rules in 2019.
